issues.title: Fix old behavior in `register_error_handler()`
issues.body:
## Background
[`Line 700 src/scaffold.py`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/f976d5bb88216e921a96998f767df31d7039e4ef/src/flask/scaffold.py#L700) has a comment `# old broken behavior`.  
```python
if isinstance(code_or_exception, HTTPException):  # old broken behavior
    raise ValueError(
        "Tried to register a handler for an exception instance"
        f" {code_or_exception!r}. Handlers can only be"
        " registered for exception classes or HTTP error codes."
    )
```
The purpose of this code is check if the handler is an exception instance.   
If so, raise an error to warn the user: the handler should be HTTPException classes or HTTP error codes.   
### Trigger test case: 
In [`test/test_user_error_handler.py`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/f976d5bb88216e921a96998f767df31d7039e4ef/tests/test_user_error_handler.py), add:
```python
with pytest.raises(ValueError):
    app.register_error_handler(HTTPException(), None)
```
### Why is this old and broken?  
From version 0.7, `self.register_error_handler` can accept all `Exception` not just `HTTPException` so it is not accurate now. Also, the main check part for handlers is in `self._get_exc_class_and_code`.

## Purposed Solution
Remove this part of code.  
Enhance the check for handlers in `self.register_error_handler`.  

## Detail Discussion
- Since the main check is in `self._get_exc_class_and_code`, new check part is written in `self._get_exc_class_and_code` to keep consistency.
- `isinstance(exc_class, Exception)` is kept for warning error-prone cases.
- Idea from [`inspect.isclass`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/inspect.html#inspect.isclass) to solve `Line 735 scr/scaffold.py` `TypeError: issubclass() arg 1 must be a class` when arg1 is a instance.  
This idea uses `New-style Classes` feature in Python3. Since Flask needs Python>=3.7, it should not cause any compatibility issues.
- Move `except KeyError` after confirm `int` type to improve type safety.
- Print `exc_class` when AssertionError to improve traceback.

A PR will be linked.

issues.title: asserts with `pytest.raises` should be outside the `with` block
issues.body:
I've been using Flask's test suite to evaluate our [Slipcover](https://github.com/plasma-umass/slipcover) coverage tool and noticed likely bugs in the Flask tests.  For example, in `tests/test_basic.py`, you have

```python
def test_response_type_errors():
    [...]

    with pytest.raises(TypeError) as e:
        c.get("/none")
        assert "returned None" in str(e.value)
        assert "from_none" in str(e.value)

    with pytest.raises(TypeError) as e:
        c.get("/small_tuple")
        assert "tuple must have the form" in str(e.value)

    [...]

    with pytest.raises(TypeError) as e:
        c.get("/bad_type")
        assert "it was a bool" in str(e.value)
```
You probably don't want the `assert` statements checking `e` indented, as they won't execute when the exception is thrown.

issues.title: reqparse fails on multipart/form-data due to change in werkzeug.request
issues.body:
when some `multipart/form-data` request is parsed via a` reqparse.RequestParser()`, the parsing fails with 

> werkzeug.exceptions.BadRequest: 400 Bad Request: Did not attempt to load JSON data because the request Content-Type was not 'application/json'.

To replicate create some endpoint, which parses the request with a `reqparse.RequestParser` and send the requested data as `multipart/form-data` for example with `curl`. 

With flask version 2.0.2 (and a corresponding older werkzeug version m(i.e. <2.1.1) ), this worked as expected, i.e. the request gets parsed correctly, with flask version 2.1.1 and werkzeug 2.1.1 (or newer) it fails.

This happens, because with werkzeug version 2.1.1, werkzeug the behaviour of request.get_json() was changes:

"Request.get_json() will raise a 400 BadRequest error if the Content-Type header is not application/json. This makes a very common source of confusion more visible. #2339"

(c.f. https://werkzeug.palletsprojects.com/en/2.1.x/changes/ or https://github.com/pallets/werkzeug/issues/2339)

`requparse.Argument` now loads its location as default with

```
location=('json', 'values',)
```
in line 77 of the `__init__` function and then iterates over `self.location` (in line 125f):
```
for l in self.location:
                value = getattr(request, l, None)
```
which access `request.json` (first) and then  fails due to the new exception in/from werkzeug. 

Capturing that exception or accessing json only if the application type matches json would prevent that error and would allow to continue to use the reqparse with application types not being json.

issues.title: Is it a bug ?
Fuzzing integration by way of OSS-Fuzz
issues.body:
Hi,

Given the popularity of flask I was thinking that it would be nice to set up continuous fuzzing of flask by way of OSS-Fuzz. In this PR: https://github.com/google/oss-fuzz/pull/7542 I have done exactly that, namely created the necessary logic from an OSS-Fuzz perspective to integrate flask. This includes developing an initial two fuzzers as well as the necessary glue for working with OSS-Fuzz. Down the line it is preferable to have the fuzzers upstream but it can be convenient to have on OSS-Fuzz to begin with.

Essentially, OSS-Fuzz is a free service run by Google that performs continuous fuzzing of important open source projects. The only expectation of integrating into OSS-Fuzz is that bugs will be fixed. This is not a "hard" requirement in that no one enforces this and the main point is if bugs are not fixed then it is a waste of resources to run the fuzzers, which we would like to avoid. The fuzzing set up on the OSS-Fuzz side relies on Atheris fuzzer to perform the fuzzing.

If you would like to integrate, the only thing I need is as list of email(s) that will get access to the data produced by OSS-Fuzz, such as bug reports, coverage reports and more stats. Notice the emails affiliated with the project will be public in the OSS-Fuzz repo, as they will be part of a configuration file.

issues.title: `flask.safe_join` Was Removed Without A Clear Deprecation Notice
issues.body:
In version 2.1.1, `flask.safe_join` was removed. However, the [documentation for version 2.0.x](https://flask.palletsprojects.com/en/2.0.x/api/#flask.safe_join) did not include any deprecation notice. 

A deprecation warning _was_ raised when calling `safe_join` in version 2.0.x, but many developers rely on the documentation for deprecation notices. Also, the warning referred explicitly only to `flask.helpers.safe_join`, and not to `flask.safe_join`, so it made sense to assume that the shorthand `flask.safe_join` will continue to exist (wrapping `werkzeug.utils.safe_join` instead of `flask.helpers.safe_join`).

I suppose many developers were surprised like me from the change, and hence many applications broke after a Flask upgrade (or will break soon, when they upgrade).

To mitigate this problem, I suggest `flask.safe_join` is reintroduced for version 2.1.x (and as soon as possible), while a clear deprecation notice is added to the documentation.

issues.title: `flaskr` docs use raw SQL statements in SQLAlchemy
issues.body:
Hello everyone and thanks for this project, especially the fantastic documentations!

In [this part of the documentation](https://flask.palletsprojects.com/en/2.0.x/tutorial/views/#the-first-view-register), the `flaskr` example application handles authentication mechanisms by inserting new users / authenticating existing users by connecting to a SQLite database. It uses raw string statements to register new users and/or authenticate them.

Of course, this is an example application, but SQLAlchemy offers database statements as objects which have several benefits as:

- SQL injection safety
- Database actions _as code_

The tutorial does in this case not show the optimal code regarding database statement executions. 

New(er) programmers might not just make their first steps in web application programming using Python Flask, but maybe even make their first steps connecting to a database. I'd propose to rather use a code snippet similar to this:

```python
# code snippet for registering a new user
users = Table('users', metadata, autoload=True)
stmt = users.insert()
stmt.execute(username=username, password=generate_password_hash(password))
```

This way, one does not think about writing raw SQL statements and writes safe code by default.

Thank you and have a nice day!

issues.title: `app.route` and similar decorators can have better types
issues.body:
Currently, `@app.route` creates a decorator function that takes in a `t.Callable` and returns a `t.Callable`.

This leads to type erasure:

```python
import flask

def foo() -> bool:
    return True

reveal_type(foo)

app = flask.Flask(__name__)

@app.route('/bar')
def bar() -> bool:
    return True

reveal_type(bar)
```

```console
$ mypy mycode.py
mycode.py:6: note: Revealed type is "def () -> builtins.bool"
mycode.py:14: note: Revealed type is "Any"
```

Although the function still works the same way:

```pycon
>>> foo()
True
>>> bar()
True
```

Replacing `t.Callable` in the code with a bound `TypeVar` should allow mypy to infer that the decorator shouldn't change the types of the function.

issues.title: TaggedJSONSerializer doesn't round-trip naive datetimes
issues.body:
Since https://github.com/pallets/werkzeug/commit/265bad7, `parse_date` always returns an aware datetime. This can't be compared with naive datetimes, so will break a bunch of existing code.

```
>>> from flask.json.tag import TaggedJSONSerializer
>>> s = TaggedJSONSerializer()
>>> datetime.utcnow()
datetime.datetime(2022, 2, 25, 1, 52, 43, 79586)
>>> s.loads(s.dumps(datetime.utcnow()))
datetime.datetime(2022, 2, 25, 1, 52, 44, tzinfo=datetime.timezone.utc)
```

This probably makes sense for werkzeug, but not for a JSON serialiser.

It might be enough to replace the calls to `http_date` and `parse_date` with `value.isoformat()` and `datetime.fromisoformat(value)`, which will work fine for aware and naive datetimes.

Environment:

- Python version: 3.9
- Flask version: 2.0.2

issues.body:
In the [Sending Requests with the Test Client](https://flask.palletsprojects.com/en/2.0.x/testing/#sending-requests-with-the-test-client) section of the documentation it's said that:

> The `client` has methods that match the common HTTP request methods, such as `client.get()` and `client.post()`. They take many arguments for building the request; you can find the full documentation in [EnvironBuilder](https://werkzeug.palletsprojects.com/en/2.0.x/test/#werkzeug.test.EnvironBuilder). Typically you’ll use `path`, `query`, `headers`, and `data` or `json`.

And also:

> Pass a dict `query={"key": "value", ...}` to set arguments in the query string (after the ? in the URL). Pass a dict `headers={}` to set request headers.

But looking at the linked [EnvironBuilder class](https://werkzeug.palletsprojects.com/en/2.0.x/test/#werkzeug.test.EnvironBuilder) it's clear that there is no `query` parameter, but rather `query_string`, which does not take a `dict`. def create_app(*args, **kwargs):

    script_info = ctx.obj if ctx else None
    ...
```

`manage.py`
```python
import click

from flask.cli import FlaskGroup, pass_script_info

from app import create_app


@click.group(cls=FlaskGroup, create_app=create_app)
@click.option("-m", "--config-mode", default="Development")

def manager(script_info, config_mode=None, **kwargs):

issues.title: Missing type annotation on `Flask.session_interface`
issues.body:
https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/main/src/flask/app.py#L377-L381

This leads type checkers (`mypy` in our case) to complain if we try to assign something to `session_interface` that isn't `SecureCookieSessionInterface`, even if it implements `SessionInterface`.

To reproduce, create a custom session interface that extends `SessionInterface`. Set `Flask.session_interface` to an instance of this. Then run `mypy` on this file.

The type annotation should allow other session interface implementations to be used.

issues.title: Use `render_template("...", as_string=True, **ctx)` instead of `render_template_string("...", **ctx)`
docs: Potentially promoting poor security practise for credentials validation
issues.body:
In [here](https://flask.palletsprojects.com/en/2.0.x/testing/#logging-in-and-out) we have

```python
def test_login_logout(client):
    """Make sure login and logout works."""

    username = flaskr.app.config["USERNAME"]
    password = flaskr.app.config["PASSWORD"]

    rv = login(client, username, password)
    assert b'You were logged in' in rv.data

    rv = logout(client)
    assert b'You were logged out' in rv.data

    rv = login(client, f"{username}x", password)
    assert b'Invalid username' in rv.data

    rv = login(client, username, f'{password}x')
    assert b'Invalid password' in rv.data
```

Telling exactly whether the name or the password was wrong is frowned upon as it gives the attacker the ability to see whether or not a user exists in the database. The docs though for a toy app gives the impression that it is how an app should be developed.

issues.title: github_link uses suboptimal shortcut
issues.body:
On Line 91 of root/docs/conf.py, it says `options = options or {}`

It is trying to use the fact that options is initialized to None, which is falsy, to then initialize it to {}. 

However, this means that if you call github_link with options being some other falsy value (0, for example), rather than giving an error,  it will quietly initialize it to {}. This could potentially hide a bug in a caller of the function. 

An easy fix would be to replace it with: 
`if options is None:
     options = {}`

<!--
Describe how to replicate the bug.

Include a minimal reproducible example that demonstrates the bug.
Include the full traceback if there was an exception.
-->

You can replicate the bug by simply calling github_link with options = 0. 

<!--
Describe the expected behavior that should have happened but didn't.
-->

The expected behavior would be for the function to give an error. Instead, it silently corrects it to {}. 

Environment:

- Python version: Any
- Flask version:  Latest (2.0.2)

Flask not sanitising arrays in JSON input

Include a minimal reproducible example that demonstrates the bug.

issues.title: Lazy blueprint loading feature request
issues.body:
Lately I have been profiling my unit tests, and I found that the flask application loading in my unit test fixtures is very costly. All the blueprint tree must be loaded, and all their dependencies, even if I test one single view. This brings my very capable machine to load a single unit test in several seconds. Thus, I would like to improve my project performances at import time.

[The documentation](https://flask.palletsprojects.com/en/2.0.x/patterns/lazyloading) shows a snippet for lazy view loading. I think this is very interesting, but this have some drawbacks. The main one being that this does not take advantage of the blueprints, and all the code mutualization they can bring.

I find this would be awesome if `register_blueprint` could also take strings as `blueprint` argument, so the blueprint modules would be imported at the last moment:

```python
# so we could replace this
import web.foobar
app.register_blueprint(web.foobar, url_prefix="/foobar")

# by this
app.register_blueprint("web.foobar.bp", url_prefix="/foobar")
```

I would be volunteer to tackle this if you think this is a good idea.

What do you think?

issues.title: Undocumented dependency on pkg_resources
issues.body:
The `flask` CLI uses `pkg_resources` (a part of `setuptools`) to detect plugin-provided subcommands, and fails silently when it's not available (see [here](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/fdac8a5404e3e3a316568107a293f134707c75bb/src/flask/cli.py#L498)). This isn't usually an issue because most environments will have pip, and therefore setuptools and pkg_resources, installed, but it does cause issues when in a hermetic environment, like Nix (see https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/pull/155245) or a sufficiently fancy Docker container. It would be nice to make the soft dependency explicit, maybe as a setup.py extra, or even make it a hard dependency.

I'm not sure this fully qualifies as a bug, but I don't really know where else to report this, so here it is.

issues.title: don't recommend using `X-XSS-Protection`
issues.body:
The [security page](https://flask.palletsprojects.com/en/2.0.x/security/) of the docs recommends using X-XSS-Protection to prevent against XSS attacks. However, this is no longer recommended since it protects only against extremely rudimentary XSS attacks while at the same time causing while new types of more difficult to prevent XSS attacks.

See [OWASP](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cross_Site_Scripting_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html#x-xss-protection-header) and [MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/X-XSS-Protection) for reasons why this is a problem.

This section should at least include a warning in case someone blindly copy pastes that code.

issues.title: Slow json loading under pypy
issues.body:
For large chunks of JSON data, the following snippet (in e.g. any post request) is very slow under pypy:
```python
request.get_json()
```
in fact it's 4x slower than doing
```python
import json
json.loads(request.get_data())
```

## Expected behaviour

I would expect using the default `get_json` to be the happy path and be as fast as the in-built `json.loads`.

## Underlying cause

I tracked this down to the use of the custom `JSONDecoder` class here: https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/main/src/flask/json/__init__.py#L53
Essentially pypy has a fast-path for the default `json.loads` - and if you use a hand-rolled decoder class you don't get to use that fast path.
Note that the `JSONDecoder` class does nothing except add some docstrings, but it's very hard for pypy to know that without some horrible introspection of the decoder class every time you call json.loads.

## Possible fix

Only set a custom `cls=` in `flask.json.load(s)` if something other than the default is set on `app.json_decoder`.


## Environment:

- Python version: pypy3.7
- Flask version: 2.0.2

issues.title: Domain detected by `ProxyFix` not applied to session cookie
issues.body:
I have a small Flask website behind a CDN. I use the Werkzeug `ProxyFix` to detect the user-facing hostname by parsing the `X-Forwarded-Host` header. It works fine, absolute URLs are generated by prefixing the user-facing hostname instead of the origin hostname the CDN uses the fetch and cache the pages.

Unfortunately this doesn't seem to be the case for the `domain` part of the session cookie. I'm running with default configuration. The `domain` part of the session cookie contains the origin hostname, that the CDN passes unchanged (correct behavior for a CDN) and the browser then discards, because it doesn't match the hostname it sees.

It looks like the session domain is calculated once at Flask application initialization time, before this application object is wrapped by `ProxyFix`. Note also that the user-facing hostname can't be known at Flask app startup time, because it's passed in requests header. Potentially, it could have a different value for each requests (if the same app is behind different CDN endpoints).

Nevertheless I think the issue should be fixed, or at least `ProxyFix` declared not compatible with session cookies, or the limitation clearly documented.

The problem is probably not limited to session cookies, but affects cookies in general.

Environment:

- Python version: 3.7
- Flask version: 2.0

Workaround:

Set the hostnames and domains manually. Then I don't see the reason to use of `ProxyFix`.

issues.title: Flask should ship with upper bound dependancies as well as lower bound dependancies
issues.body:
Today, if we want to install an old release of Flask, (ie 0.12.4), the pip resolver will download and setup the last version of Werkzeug, which is incompatible : https://stackoverflow.com/a/65684861

Real example that is unable to be installed today : https://github.com/ElasticHQ/elasticsearch-HQ/blob/master/requirements.txt

Please note that this problem was submitted by a user that knows well Elasticsearch, but has really light knowledge of Python.

The same problem is still possible given the fact that dependancies in Flask are not upper bounded. So any dependancies that introduce a non backward compatible change in their API will break new Flask install. Givent the fact that most projects use semantic versionning, it's easy to find an appropriate upper bound that will avoid such case.

Example : 

` install_requires=[
        "Werkzeug >= 2.0",
        "Jinja2 >= 3.0",
        "itsdangerous >= 2.0",
        "click >= 8.0",
    ],
`

should be replaced by :

` install_requires=[
        "Werkzeug >= 2.0, <3",
        "Jinja2 >= 3.0, <4",
        "itsdangerous >= 2.0, <3",
        "click >= 8.0, <9",
    ],
`

when the dependancy maintainer state that they'll respect semantic versionning.

If the depandancy in its newer version is found to not break anything, the upper bound can be set to the new major version.

issues.title: Blueprint.errorhandler restricts type of result function which avoids chaining
issues.body:
In flask 2.0.1 it was possible to chain multiple uses of `Blueprint.errorhandler` as a decorator. In 2.0.2 the type of `Blueprint.errorhandler` is too strict to allow this. Let's assume you start out with a plain handler function of type `ErrorHandlerCallable[Exception]` or similar, applying `some_blueprint.errorhandler(SomeExceptionA)` to it, changes the type of the handler to `ErrorHandlerCallable[SomeExceptionA]`. Applying `some_blueprint.errorHandler(SomeExceptionB)` is now no longer possible, because it expects a `ErrorHandlerCallable[SomeExceptionB]` which the existing error handler cannot fullfill.

Consider this example program:

```Python
from flask import Blueprint

blueprint = Blueprint('example', __name__)

class ExceptionA(Exception):
    pass

class ExceptionB(Exception):
    pass

@blueprint.errorhandler(ExceptionB)
@blueprint.errorhandler(ExceptionA)
def error(e):
    return "example"
```

with flask 2.0.1 this typechecked, with flask 2.0.2 I get the following error:

```
$ mypy test.py
test.py:11: error: Argument 1 has incompatible type "ErrorHandlerCallable[ExceptionA]"; expected "ErrorHandlerCallable[ExceptionB]"
Found 1 error in 1 file (checked 1 source file)
```

I would expect this example to work in 2.0.2 just as well as it did in 2.0.1.

I think the semantically most correct way to fix this, would be to to give `errorhandler` a type smilar to `Callable[[SomeOtherGenericException], Callable[[ErrorHandlerCallable[GenericException]], ErrorHandlerCallable[GenericException]]` where `SomeOtherGenericException` would be a type variable that would always need to be a subtype of `GenericException`, but I am not sure if Python's type system can express relations between type variables like that.

Environment:

- Python version: 3.9.7
- Flask version: 2.0.2

issues.title: MethodView Decorators list execution order
issues.body:
Hello, I was experimenting with the option to add decorators to a view via the `decorators` class variable, which contains the list of the different decorators. ([Flask docs - decorating views](https://flask.palletsprojects.com/en/2.0.x/views/#decorating-views))

So in order to decorate a MethodView method, we can't do this:
```python
# Example 1
class Example(MethodView):
    @user_required
    @data_required
    def get(self):
        ...
```
But we must do this instead:
```python
# Example 2
class Example(MethodView):
    decorators = [user_required, data_required]
    def get(self):
        ...
```
This is totally fine, but there is an issue with the way it has been implemented.

The natural order of decorators (or should I say wrapper) execution is from top to bottom.
In my first example (the natural way you would decorate a function) you suppose the code in the first decorator (`user_required`) to be executed first and then the code from the second decorator (`data_required`) → `user_required(data_required(view))`.

The thing is in the implementation of the `decorators` class variable the decorators in the list are applied in the wrong (or unnatural) order:
```python
# from Flask source code (views.py -> View class)
if cls.decorators:
    ...
    for decorator in cls.decorators:
        view = decorator(view)
```
This will execute the second decorator (`data_required`) before the first one in the list (`user_required`) which is very confusing and unnatural → `data_required(user_required(view))`.

Just imagine that the first decorator (`user_required`) exposes the `user` variable to the `g` variable (`g.user`).
The second decorator (`data_required`) pulls data from the user but as it is implemented, this would throw an error as the `user_required` decorator hasn't been executed yet.

I suggest reversing the order of the decorators before applying them to the view method:
```python
if cls.decorators:
    ...
    for decorator in revesed(cls.decorators):
        view = decorator(view)
```
It would feel more natural and lead to less confusion...

issues.title: Implementation of custom methods in blueprints
issues.body:
<!--
Replace this comment with a description of what the feature should do.
Include details such as links to relevant specs or previous discussions.
-->

I am following this guide to make my API as simple and standard as possible:
https://cloud.google.com/apis/design/custom_methods

I see this method is quite common as also I could found it at [API Design Patterns](https://www.manning.com/books/api-design-patterns) and it has sense.

However, I see currently in a flask blueprint it is not possible to use ':' separator for the root path resources.
For example:

```py
from flask.views import MethodView
from flaskimport Blueprint

blp = Blueprint('benchmarks', 'benchmarks')

@blp.route('')
class Benchmarks(MethodView)

    def get(self, query_args):
        ....
  
    def post(self, body_args):
        ....
```

This would create the following routes:
- GET /benchmarks
- POST /benchmarks

However, there is no simple way to create the following routes inside the blueprint:
- GET /benchmarks:search
- POST /benchmarks:my_custom_method


<!--
Replace this comment with an example of the problem which this feature
would resolve. Is this problem solvable without changes to Flask, such
as by subclassing or using an extension?
-->

The main issue relies here
https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/main/src/flask/blueprints.py#L93
where the only available separator after the blueprint url_prefix is '/', leading to strange combinations:
- GET /benchmarks/:search
- POST /benchmarks/:custom

Why not to use a resource path?
If I configure the following route:

- GET /benchmarks/search
Then it might conflict with my id resource

- GET /benchmarks/<string:name>
Threfore I cannot create a benchmark with name "search".
This is a design issue, the ':' convention was created to avoid this type of issues.

Solution?
Maybe just accept the ':' as an optional start character?
```py

        if self.url_prefix is not None:
            if not rule:
                rule = self.url_prefix
            elif rule[0] == ':' and 'somethingelse:
                rule =  ":".join((self.url_prefix.rstrip("/"), rule.lstrip("/")))
            else:
                rule = "/".join((self.url_prefix.rstrip("/"), rule.lstrip("/")))

```

Although there sure might be better ways.

issues.title: CRLF in Flask's headers.set method in make_response
issues.body:
A crlf bug can be triggered via the headers.set method while doing a make_response this can cause
1. Header Injection
2. Relected Xss

Describe how to replicate the bug.

```
import flask
from flask import request
from flask import make_response
app = flask.Flask(__name__)


@app.route("/")
def index():
    page = request.args.get("name")
    vals = request.args.get("vals")
    r = make_response("ASDDDF")
    r.headers.set(page, vals)
    return r

app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=8007)
```
a payload of `http://localhost:8007/?name=GET /?name=A:a%0a%0dA:d%0d%0d%0a%0dScheck&vals=dsf ` can be used to case Header Injections 

### Response
```
HTTP/1.0 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 6
A:a
A:d
Scheck: dsf
Server: Werkzeug/2.0.1 Python/3.6.9
Date: Sun, 15 Aug 2021 16:06:27 GMT

ASDDDF
```

and Similarly a payload 
```http://localhost:8007/?name=%0a%0a%3Chtml%3E%3Cscript%3Ealert(%27document.location%27)%3C/script%3Easd&val=a%0aasd```
Can Cause Xss(firefox)
### Cause
The name parameter's value (name=%0a%0a<html><script>alert('not supposed to happen')</script>) is set as the header's name. But due to no sanitization, %0a can be used to inject new headers or arbitrary HTML content.


## Describe the expected behaviour that should have happened but didn't.
%0a in the header's value is sanitized and causes no CRLF(throws 500 internal error). The same could be expected in the case of header's name.


Environment:

- Python version: 3.6.9
- Flask version: 2.0.1

issues.title: Add support for a `FLASK_RUN_EXTRA_FILES` config variable.
issues.body:
[This section of the flask documentation](https://flask.palletsprojects.com/en/2.0.x/cli/?highlight=flask_run_extra_files#watch-extra-files-with-the-reloader) discusses how you can watch additional files with the reloader. 

You can currently do this by using the `--extra_files` option of the `flask run` command. Or by setting a `FLASK_RUN_EXTRA_FILES` environment variable. 

Ideally you could bundle this in with your application config, since it's not something that's likely to change from environment to environment but is inherent to the application itself.

Currently, I work around this by hard-coding the setting of the environment variable in my development config class:

```python
class DevelopmentConfig(Config):
    DEBUG = True
    ENV = "development"
    extra_files = [os.path.join("foo","bar.txt"), os.path.join("assets","styles.scss")]
    if os.name != 'nt':
            # Posix
            os.environ["FLASK_RUN_EXTRA_FILES"] = ":".join(extra_files)
        else:
            # Windows
            os.environ["FLASK_RUN_EXTRA_FILES"] = ";".join(extra_files)
```

I'm proposing a config variable that supports a list of file paths to watch:
```python
class DevelopmentConfig(Config):
    DEBUG = True
    ENV = "development"
    FLASK_RUN_EXTRA_FILES = [os.path.join("foo","bar.txt"), os.path.join("assets","styles.scss")]
```

issues.title: `template_filter` decorator typing does not support custom filters with multiple arguments
issues.body:
`template_filter` decorator typing does not support custom filters that take in multiple arguments. Consider:

```py
from flask import Flask


app = Flask(__name__)


@app.template_filter('foo_bar')
def foo_bar_filter(foo, bar):
    return f'{foo} {bar}'
```
`mypy` will return the following error message:
```
error: Argument 1 has incompatible type "Callable[[Any, Any], Any]"; expected "Callable[[Any], str]"  [arg-type]
```
As custom filters with multiple arguments are supported by Jinja (https://jinja.palletsprojects.com/en/3.0.x/api/#custom-filters), I think this typing error is a false positive.

- Flask version: 2.0.1
- Mypy version: 0.812

issues.title: Debug reloader extra files arg doesn't accept directories
issues.body:
I'm using Webpack to bundle static assets from an "src/assets" subdirectory and place the generated files into the "src/static" directory.

I need to instruct the reloader to watch all extra files in the "src/assets" directory and reload the app on changes. 

To do this, there are three options:
* There's an environment variable `FLASK_RUN_EXTRA_FILES=...`
* There's a command line argument to `flask_run --extra-files=...`
* You can pass it as an option directly to the `app.run(extra_files=[...])` function. 

All three of these approaches do not accept directory paths, every individual file to watch must be enumerated. 

I suppose that in and of itself is a problem with Werkzeug not Flask, since it appears the options are just passed through to the `run_simple` function. 

However, because of this limitation, I need to find a good way to construct this option dynamically based on the current state of the "src/assets" directory before the app starts. 

I can't figure out how one would do this, and still be able to use the `flask run` cli command to start the server. 

So I'm proposing one of two fixes:
1) Allow the `extra_files` option to accept directory paths as inputs. This would require enumerating each of the files in the directories before passing the option to Werkzeug, or patching Werkzeug to do this. 
2) Allow the `flask_run` command to be mapped to a specific configuration of the `app.run()` function. Currently I can either configure an `app.run()` to use within the `if __name__ == "__main__":` block, however then I can no longer use the `flask run` cli command and instead need to start the application with "python main.py". 

**Minimal example**
Project structure:
```
app/
  assets/
    main.js
  main.py
```
```python
# main.py
from flask import Flask


app = Flask(__name__)

if __name__=="__main__":
	app.run(debug=1, extra_files=["./assets/"])
```
```javascript
// assets/main.js
console.log('test');
```
Run using `python main.py` or `flask run --extra-fields=./assets/`, and modify `./assets/main.js`. The server does not reload. 

Then either modify the extra_files argument of the `app.run()` command to `extra_files=["./assets/main.js"]` and re-run with `python main.py`, or run the cli command `flask run --extra-fields=./assets/main.js`. Now, if you change `./assets/main.js` the server reloads. 

**Expected Behavior**
Specifying a path to a directory watches every file in that directory.  OR
`flask_run` calls the configured `app.run(...)` function so that I can generate the list of files to watch at run time. 

**Environment:**

- Python version: 3.9.5
- Flask version: 2.0.1

issues.title: create_app factory with variable length keyword arguments raises an error
issues.body:
# Description

My `create_app` factory accepts optional variable length keyword arguments:

```
def create_app(**kwargs):
    pass
```

We use these to optionally inject pre-initialized service objects into the application, usually for testing purposes. This worked through Flask 1.1.4, but breaks due to changes regarding the `script_info` parameter made in 2.0.0.

```
Error: Detected factory 'create_app' in module 'service.main', but could not call it without arguments. Use "FLASK_APP='service.main:create_app(args)'" to specify arguments.
```

The buggy logic is in [call_factory](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/2.0.1/src/flask/cli.py#L106-L110); inspect considers the default value for a `**kwargs` argument to be empty. This causes the flask code to inject script_info as a positional argument, despite the function signature not accepting any positional args. A check needs to be added to exclude variable length kwargs, for example:

```
if (
    not args
    and len(sig.parameters) == 1
    and next(iter(sig.parameters.values())).default is inspect.Parameter.empty
    and next(iter(sig.parameters.values())).kind is not inspect.Parameter.VAR_KEYWORD
):  
```

# Test Case

Here's a test case that reproduces the bug:

```
class Module:
    @staticmethod
    def create_app(**kwargs):
        return Flask("appname")

app = find_best_app(script_info, Module)
assert isinstance(app, Flask)
assert app.name == "appname"
```

I was hoping to submit a simple patch for this issue, but the change I described above breaks tests for auto_reload and debug in ways that I don't quite understand.

```

            app.debug = True

        @cli.command()

app = <Flask 'flask_test'>, monkeypatch = <_pytest.monkeypatch.MonkeyPatch object at 0x1057ad9d0>

issues.title: Large File Uploading Issue with RAM (x/post to Werkzeug)
issues.body:
Writing this as an open-ended discussion and will be submitting the same information to the respective packages involved in this issue. Please note that this issue has been raised *several times* before, but has yet to be fixed / resolved. ([Flask #2086](https://github.com/pallets/flask/issues/2086), [Werkzeug #1041](https://github.com/pallets/werkzeug/issues/1041), [Werkzeug #510](https://github.com/pallets/werkzeug/issues/510), [Codalab-Worksheet #301](https://github.com/codalab/codalab-worksheets/issues/301), see also: [StackOverflow Question](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/28321690/python3-flask-upload-file-in-server-memory))

Currently, the [`default_stream_factory` ](https://github.com/pallets/werkzeug/blob/eff04478a83619b4d7f15e6eee16a99bd80ed879/src/werkzeug/formparser.py#L60) that is embedded in [Werkzeug](https://github.com/pallets/werkzeug) (a [Flask](https://github.com/pallets/flask) Dependency) splits files and performs one of two operations:

- If under 500kb, store the uploaded file in-memory.
- If over 500kb, store the file in a temp file in /tmp.

This creates one main *visible* problem:

- Machines with a smaller /tmp may send a traceback to the user with a "No Space on Device" OSError, not allowing uploads to complete.

And one *hidden* problem:

- Large File Uploads (>500kb as defined in [`default_stream_factory`](https://github.com/pallets/werkzeug/blob/eff04478a83619b4d7f15e6eee16a99bd80ed879/src/werkzeug/formparser.py#L66)) *still* eat into the RAM of the host machine, despite being sent to /tmp via [`TemporaryFile`](https://github.com/pallets/werkzeug/blob/eff04478a83619b4d7f15e6eee16a99bd80ed879/src/werkzeug/formparser.py#L71) or [`SpooledTemporaryFile`](https://github.com/pallets/werkzeug/blob/eff04478a83619b4d7f15e6eee16a99bd80ed879/src/werkzeug/formparser.py#L69).

This redundancy can lead to a severe issue.
I was testing NS on a 4GB machine and performing a 4GB upload, which crashed the machine, and led me do two things:

- Up my /tmp size to 10GB in `/etc/fstab`
- Investigate the Memory Leak

I've not found a fix for this or any surefire way of counteracting the problem. Despite ensuring that /tmp has more than enough storage, RAM is still consumed. If the upload eats the RAM to 100% a system crash will occur, throwing the server offline. Somewhere in the reading I've been doing it's been suggested that Werkzeug stores the files into memory regardless of size (rendering `formparser` useless?) and has sloppy management with the data.

I have confirmed that this is reproducible by uninstalling and reinstalling both Flask and Werkzeug and trying it on multiple machines.

The intended behavior (storing in /tmp and not RAM) isn't happening.

Environment:

- Python Version: 3.9.5
- Flask Version: 2.0.1

Any possible fixes or monkey patches would be appreciated; collaboration and discussion is welcome!

issues.title: handle Decimal in json encoder
issues.body:
The `simplejson` removal (#3555) decreased the flask encoding capabilities as the built-in `json` doesn't cover cases like `Decimal` types. The solution seems to be: overwrite the flask app encoder with `JSONEnconder` from `simplejson`, but this incorporates a problem for users that relies on both `Decimal` and `datetimes` as `simplejon` doesn't handle `datetimes`, while flask encoder does. The solution I found is to build a custom encoder that tests if the value is `Decimal` and gives it to `simplejson`, otherwise, handles it with the default flask app encoder. My suggestion is to incorporate a simple test in the flask encoder to add `Decimal` coverage, that would remove any residual dependency on `simplejson`. The str(decimal) was taken from: [simplejson/encoder.py#L511](https://github.com/simplejson/simplejson/blob/8bef979ad8272cbc2903970f4b9992f603d50973/simplejson/encoder.py#L511)  

```python
from flask import json as fjson
from flask.json import JSONEncoder
import simplejson as sjson
import decimal
from datetime import datetime

rdatetime = datetime.strptime('1/1/2008 1:30 PM', '%m/%d/%Y %I:%M %p')
rdecimal = decimal.Decimal(10)

obj = {'datetime':rdatetime,'decimal':rdecimal}

fjson.dumps(obj) #Doesn't work because of decimal
sjson.dumps(obj) #Doesn't work because of datetimes
```  
The custom encoder:  
```python
class CustomJSONEncoder(JSONEncoder):
    '''
    Add Decimal coverage
    '''
    def default(self, o):
        if isinstance(o, decimal.Decimal):
            return str(o)
        return super().default(o)

app.json_encoder = CustomJSONEncoder
```  

The expected behavior is to work with both `Decimal` and `datetimes`  as it used to work on Flask version 1.1.2

Environment:

- Python version: 3.8.10
- Flask version: 2.0.1 and 1.1.2
- Simplejson(Optional) version: 3.17.2

Replace this comment with a clear outline of what the bug is.
-->

Using a class based view (specifically a MethodView), if you were to save something like a list, dict, or set, as a class attribute, this would persist through different requests.

<!--
Describe how to replicate the bug.

Include a minimal reproducible example that demonstrates the bug.
Include the full traceback if there was an exception.
-->

To reproduce the bug:

```python
class MyView(MethodView):
    a_list = []
    a_dict = dict()
    a_set = set()

    def get(self):
        print(self.a_list, flush=True)
        self.a_list.append(len(self.a_list))
        print(self.a_dict, flush=True)
        self.a_dict[len(self.a_dict.keys())] = len(self.a_dict.keys())
        print(self.a_set, flush=True)
        self.a_set.add(len(self.a_set))
        return ""
```

<!--
Describe the expected behavior that should have happened but didn't.
-->

If you hit this endpoint, the first time, the list, dict, and set is printed as empty. Then if you hit the same endpoint, the three vars now show the previous requests variables. Keep hitting the endpoint and the list, dict, and set will continue growing without ever refreshing.

Environment:

- Python version: 3.8.10
- Flask version: 1.1.2

issues.title: Support of HTTP/2 cleartext (h2c) format in flask
issues.body:
From documentation it feels like flask does not support h2c (i.e. HTTP/2 in the clear, no encryption). 

I have a use cases where an L7 proxy (e.g. Envoy) is actually managing certificates and encrypted connections across the network, and the connection between the service and the proxy is just host-local. In this case, we want to achieve h2c between the proxy and the service (flask application).

Is there any way through which we can enable h2c via configuration in the flask application?
and if it is not supported now, is there any roadmap for it?

issues.title: Directly add Short Responses
issues.body:
Instead of using the decorator which is confusing to newcomers and is a bit too long to just do simple responses like:

```py
@app.route("/style.css")
def style():
    return Response("body { background-color: red; }")
```
For simple responses it should be simple and pythonic to use something like:

```py
app.add_response("/style.css", "body { background-color: red; }")
```

I don't think it should be too hard to implement (I can actually do it myself).

Unexpected behavior when deploying Flask as Azure WebApp after Flask 2.x release
issues.body:
We deploy a Dash Dashboard as Azure WebApp with mounting blob storage. where Dash pulls the latest Flask version.

This works fine but starting mid of May we faced the problem that we noticed a high number (like 10k...10M) of ListBlob Transactions were happening increasing our storage cost.

We did not find the exact root cause, but we found that the problem starts when we recreated our Docker container mid of May which then pulled Flask 2.0.1 instead of Flask 1.1.x.

We further found that the root cause may not only be Flask itself but its dependencies.
E.g. all works fine with Flask 1.1.4 which install requires defines upper limits for its required packages:
install_requires=[ "Werkzeug >= 0.15, <2.0", "Jinja2 >= 2.10.1, <3.0", "itsdangerous >= 0.24, < 2.0", "click >= 5.1, < 8.0", ]
But things break today (End of May 2021) with Flask 1.1.2 which setup.py defines no upper limits of its required packages:
install_requires=[ "Werkzeug>=0.15", "Jinja2>=2.10.1", "itsdangerous>=0.24", "click>=5.1", ]
However, Flask 1.1.2 was working for us beginning of May 2021, but in mid of May there were major version updates on Werkzeug, Jinja and Click.
We were not deep diving further on this.

This ticket I anyway put here to inform the community, eventually get feedback from others and to raise the question how Flask may handle such eventual issues with major updates on its required packages, or if Flask 2 may need similar upper bounds on some of its used packages like version 1.1.4

issues.title: Async class based view causes crash
issues.body:
## The Bug * `flask.views.View` does not properly handle conversion of an async `dispatch_request`, resulting in a coroutine that is never awaited. * `flask.views.MethodView` does not properly handle conversion of async methods, resulting in coroutines that are never awaited. ## Replication 1. Create an async `dispatch_request` method on a `View`, or a `get` method on a `MethodView`. 1. Add the view to the app using the `View.as_view()` and `app.add_url_rule()` functions. 1. Access the route and observe a crash and 500 status code. The following application reproduces the bug. ```python from flask import Flask from flask.views import View, MethodView app = Flask("MyApp") class TestAsyncView(View): async def dispatch_request(self): return 'ASYNC VIEW RESPONSE' class TestAsyncMethodView(MethodView): async def get(self): return 'ASYNC METHODVIEW GET RESPONSE' app.add_url_rule("/async_view", view_func=TestAsyncView.as_view("test_async_view")) app.add_url_rule('/async_methodview', view_func=TestAsyncMethodView.as_view('test_async_methodview')) if __name__ == "__main__": app.run(port=8000) ``` The following error occurs after running `curl localhost:8000/async_view`: ``` Traceback (most recent call last): File "/Users/tpansino/NewRelic/Testing/Flask2Bug/flask/src/flask/app.py", line 2073, in wsgi_app response = self.full_dispatch_request() File "/Users/tpansino/NewRelic/Testing/Flask2Bug/flask/src/flask/app.py", line 1519, in full_dispatch_request return self.finalize_request(rv) File "/Users/tpansino/NewRelic/Testing/Flask2Bug/flask/src/flask/app.py", line 1538, in finalize_request response = self.make_response(rv) File "/Users/tpansino/NewRelic/Testing/Flask2Bug/flask/src/flask/app.py", line 1730, in make_response raise TypeError( TypeError: The view function did not return a valid response. The return type must be a string, dict, tuple, Response instance, or WSGI callable, but it was a coroutine. ``` ``` 500 Internal Server Error

Internal Server Error

The server encountered an internal error and was unable to complete your request. Either the server is overloaded or there is an error in the application.

``` ## Expected Behavior * Asynchronous `dispatch_request` functions and methods should either be: * Converted using `async_to_sync` before being returned from `as_view()`. * Executed or awaited in the application when a route is accessed. ## Environment - Python version: 3.9.5 - Flask version: 2.0.1

issues.title: Registering same blueprints multiple of time with different name doesn't bring blueprint's registered error handler and before request logic with it
issues.body:
Prior to version Flask 2.0.2, it was possible to register blueprints multiple of times with different url prefix during Flask App factory. Such as:
```
    # Flask 0.10.1
    from my_project.api.v1.user import user_api_v1
    app.register_blueprint(user_api_v1,
                           url_prefix='/api/latest/users')
    app.register_blueprint(user_api_v1,
                           url_prefix='/api/v1/users')

    from my_project.api.v1.recipe import recipe_api_v1
    app.register_blueprint(recipe_api_v1,
                           url_prefix='/api/latest/recipes')
    app.register_blueprint(recipe_api_v1,
                           url_prefix='/api/v1/recipes')
```

But with latest Flask version, the above was updated into this:

```
    from my_project.api.v1.user import user_api_v1
    app.register_blueprint(user_api_v1,
                           name='users_latest',
                           url_prefix='/api/latest/users')
    app.register_blueprint(user_api_v1,
                           name='users_v1',
                           url_prefix='/api/v1/users')

    from my_project.api.v1.recipe import recipe_api_v1
    app.register_blueprint(recipe_api_v1,
                           name='recipes_latest',
                           url_prefix='/api/latest/recipes')
    app.register_blueprint(recipe_api_v1,
                           name='recipes_v1',
                           url_prefix='/api/v1/recipes')
```

Basically, adding unique `name`. However, this change caused an issue that the error- and before_request-handlers that was registered to blueprints do not get mapped to the second blueprint.

This was the result for the new Flask App:
```
# App's url map
Map([<Rule '/api/latest/recipes/' (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) -> recipes_latest.get_all>,
 <Rule '/api/latest/users/' (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) -> users_latest.get_all>,
 <Rule '/api/v1/recipes/' (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) -> recipes_v1.get_all>,
 <Rule '/api/v1/users/' (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) -> users_v1.get_all>,
 <Rule '/api/latest/recipes/<id>' (POST, OPTIONS) -> recipes_latest.post>,
 <Rule '/api/v1/recipes/<id>' (POST, OPTIONS) -> recipes_v1.post>,
 <Rule '/api/latest/recipes/<id>' (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) -> recipes_latest.get>,
 <Rule '/api/v1/recipes/<id>' (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) -> recipes_v1.get>,
 <Rule '/static/<filename>' (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) -> static>])

# App's before_request_funcs
defaultdict(<class 'list'>,
            {None: [<function requires_staff_permission at 0x7fe42b9be840>],
             'recipes_latest': [<function _require_chef_permission at 0x7fe429a67f28>],
             'users_latest': [<function _require_manager_permission at 0x7fe42acb90d0>]})

# App's error_handler_spec
defaultdict(<function Scaffold.__init__.<locals>.<lambda> at 0x7fe42ad0aa60>,
            {None: defaultdict(<class 'dict'>,
                               {None: {<class 'Exception'>: <function generic_error_handler.<locals>.error_handler at 0x7fe42ad0ab70>}}),
             'recipes_latest': defaultdict(<class 'dict'>,
                                           {None: {<class 'my_project.api.v1.recipe.MissingParameter'>: <function handle_missing_argument at 0x7fe429a68510>,
                                                   <class 'my_project.api.v1.recipe.MongoDocumentNotFound'>: <function handle_no_mongo_document at 0x7fe429a68400>,
                                                   <class 'my_project.api.v1.recipe.UnsupportedParameter'>: <function handle_invalid_argument at 0x7fe429a68488>}}),
             'users_latest': defaultdict(<class 'dict'>,
                                         {None: {<class 'my_project.api.v1.user.UnsupportedParameter'>: <function handle_invalid_argument at 0x7fe42acb92f0>}})})
```
What this means is that when request is done to `GET /api/v1`, it will not trigger any handlers, because handlers are registered to `x_latest` and `/api/v1` was registered with `x_v1` blueprint name.

The behaviour I'd expect after using `app.register_blueprint` for same blueprint object with different name is that the new registered name should also have same registered error- and before request-handler mapped like so:

```
# Expected App's before_request_funcs
defaultdict(<class 'list'>,
            {None: [<function requires_staff_permission at 0x7fe42b9be840>],
             'recipes_latest': [<function _require_chef_permission at 0x7fe429a67f28>],
             'recipes_v1': [<function _require_chef_permission at 0x7fe429a67f28>],
             'users_latest': [<function _require_manager_permission at 0x7fe42acb90d0>],
             'users_v1': [<function _require_manager_permission at 0x7fe42acb90d0>]})

# Expected App's error_handler_spec
defaultdict(<function Scaffold.__init__.<locals>.<lambda> at 0x7fe42ad0aa60>,

issues.title: View and MethodView classes do not support async handlers
issues.body:
Regular views can now be written as async functions, but instances of the `View` and `MethodView` classes did not get updated to support this functionality. Consider the following example:

```python
import asyncio
from flask import Flask
from flask.views import View, MethodView

app = Flask(__name__)

class Test(View):
    async def dispatch_request(self):
        await asyncio.sleep(1)
        return 'test'

class Test2(MethodView):
    async def get(self):
        await asyncio.sleep(1)
        return 'test2'

app.add_url_rule('/test', view_func=Test.as_view('test'))
app.add_url_rule('/test2', view_func=Test2.as_view('test2'))
```

The expectation is that you should be able to send requests to `/test` and `/test2` and that their respective handlers should be wrapped with the `app.ensure_sync()` method, as function-based handlers are.

Instead sending requests to these URLs cause the following error:

```
TypeError: The view function did not return a valid response. The return type must be a string, dict, tuple, Response instance, or WSGI callable, but it was a coroutine.
```

Environment:

- Python version: >= 3.7
- Flask version: >= 2

issues.body:
Howdy! I've been working a lot with Flask (1.1.2) recently and have been running into a bug when installing Flask on devices running python2.7. Flask installs Werkzeug>=2.0 as one of its dependencies, however past version 1.0.x, [Werkzeug only supports python3.6+](https://werkzeug.palletsprojects.com/en/2.0.x/installation/). As a result, Werkzeug installs the dataclasses module, which produces syntax errors when run in python2.7. To resolve this, Flask may have to downgrade the version of Werkzeug that it uses to one that offers python2.7 support (ex: 1.0.x)

For reference, here is where Flask expects an ImportError when trying to use dataclasses python < 3.7, but instead gets a SyntaxError because Werkzeug installs the dataclasses module.

https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/7161776824734fc2797fe2b4fc974d183487ebf8/src/flask/json/__init__.py#L18-L22

### How to Replicate
Run `pip install flask>=1.1.2` on a device with python2.7

### Expected Behaviour
Should be able to install and import flask on devices running python2.7

Environment:

- Python version: 2.7.12
- Flask version: 1.1.2

issues.title: Wrong typing for `before_request` decorator
issues.body:
The [doc](https://flask.palletsprojects.com/en/2.0.x/api/#flask.Flask.before_request) says the following:
```
The function will be called without any arguments. 
If it returns a non-None value, the value is handled 
as if it was the return value from the view, and further 
request handling is stopped.
```
However the function type hint is not correct:
https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/7161776824734fc2797fe2b4fc974d183487ebf8/src/flask/typing.py#L38

I guess it's because this type was used not only for `before_request` but for `before_first_request`, `before_app_request` and `before_app_first_request` decorators too. But that's what `before_first_request` [doc](https://flask.palletsprojects.com/en/2.0.x/api/#flask.Flask.before_first_request) says:
```
The function will be called without any arguments and its return value is ignored.
```

Maybe existing `BeforeRequestCallable` type should be renamed to `BeforeFirstRequestCallable` and used for only `before_first_request` and `before_app_first_request` decorators and there should be separate type `BeforeRequestCallable` for `before_request` and `before_app_request` decorators?

Environment:

- Python version: 3.9.5
- Flask version: 2.0.1

issues.title: Harmless race condition in tutorial
issues.body:
I was browsing the flaskr tutorial when I noticed an (admittedly quite unlikely) race condition in the `register` view, specifically:

```py
if not username:
    error = 'Username is required.'
elif not password:
    error = 'Password is required.'
elif db.execute(
    'SELECT id FROM user WHERE username = ?', (username,)
).fetchone() is not None:
    error = f"User {username} is already registered."

if error is None:
    db.execute(
        'INSERT INTO user (username, password) VALUES (?, ?)',
        (username, generate_password_hash(password))
    )
    db.commit()
    return redirect(url_for('auth.login'))
```

If two requests arrive with the right timing, the following can happen:

```
   Request 1:                                Request 2:
SELECT id
  FROM user
 WHERE username = abc
     |
     v
empty, no such user

                                          SELECT id
                                            FROM user
                                           WHERE username = abc
                                               |
                                               v
                                          empty, no such user

INSERT INTO user (username, password)
     VALUES (abc, 123)
     |
     v
    ok

                                          INSERT INTO user (username, password)
                                               VALUES (abc, 456)
                                               |
                                               v
                                          failed UNIQUE constraint -> 
                                          -> sqlite3.IntegrityError ->
                                          -> user gets HTTP 500
```

While the likelihood of this happening is pretty small and the harm practically zero (user gets HTTP 500 and has to manually login/choose a different username), I feel like this is not really the sort of good practice the tutorial should teach. I also believe it's important the developer understands that it's the UNIQUE constraint that ensures their app works correctly and not the if condition in the application code (the tutorial mentions SQL injection attacks and explains what protects the developer against them, so I don't really feel this is out of scope).

In my own app I've modified the code to the following:
```py
if not username:
    error = 'Username is required.'
elif not password:
    error = 'Password is required.'
else:
    try:
        db.execute(
            'INSERT INTO users (username, password) VALUES (?, ?)',
            (username, generate_password_hash(password))
        )
        db.commit()
    except IntegrityError:
        error = f"User {username} is already registered."
    else:
        return redirect(url_for('auth.login'))
```

I suggest something similar be incorporated into the tutorial, with a short explanation (maybe a comment) of how the UNIQUE constraint does the work for the developer and maybe a note about the principle that one should "ask forgiveness, not permission." I'm not sure on how it's better worded, so I'm making this an issue instead of a pull request.

Cheers, and thank you for your great work!

issues.title: Typing requires template globals to accept no arguments
issues.body:
The typings in Flask 2.0.1 require a function decorated with `@app.template_global()` to take no arguments. As far as I’m aware, template globals certainly are supposed to take arguments (e.g. the [example in the API documentation](https://flask.palletsprojects.com/en/2.0.x/api/#flask.Flask.template_global) takes one argument), so I assume this is not intended. I think this specific issue was introduced with #4071, which applied the `TemplateGlobalCallable` type alias to that decorator; however, the `TemplateGlobalCallable` type itself is already an alias for `t.Callable[[], t.Any]` (i.e., take no arguments and return anything) in Flask 2.0.0. I haven’t checked yet if `app.add_template_global()` is affected.

Example code:

```python
import flask


app = flask.Flask(__name__)


@app.template_global()
def identity(arg: str) -> str:
    return arg
```

> app.py:7: error: Argument 1 has incompatible type "Callable[[str], str]"; expected "Callable[[], Any]"
> Found 1 error in 1 file (checked 1 source file)

Sample repository: https://github.com/lucaswerkmeister/repro-flask-mypy-template_global

Steps to reproduce:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/lucaswerkmeister/repro-flask-mypy-template_global
make -C repro-flask-mypy-template_global
```

Environment:

- Python version: 3.9.5
- Flask version: 2.0.1
- Mypy version: 0.812

issues.title: Improve typing for `errorhandler` decorator.
issues.body:
Today the `errorhandler` decorator does not have consistency between the type of error in its parameter and the parameter of the function it is wrapping although those should be the same.

The following code should be properly typed:
```py
@app.errorhandler(auth.ExpiredTokenException)
def expired_token(error: auth.ExpiredTokenException) -> Tuple[str, int]:
    """Handle the 498 error."""

    return error.description or i18n.flask_translate("Expired token"), 498
```

the current version enforces it to be typed as
```py
@app.errorhandler(auth.ExpiredTokenException)
def expired_token(untyped_error: Exception) -> Tuple[str, int]:
    """Handle the 498 error."""

    error = typing.cast(auth.ExpiredTokenException, untyped_error)
    return error.description or i18n.flask_translate("Expired token"), 498
```

issues.title: Typing error with current_app when subclassing Flask
issues.body:
### Outline of the issue

Typing error when subclassing Flask and getting the app with `current_app`.

According to the [docs](https://flask.palletsprojects.com/en/2.0.x/patterns/subclassing/):
> The Flask class is designed for subclassing.

But mypy doesn't seem to understand that `current_app` can return one subclass of `Flask`, and that these subclasses can have new arbitrary attributes, so it raises an error.

```bash
$ mypy src
src/cat.py:3: error: "Flask" has no attribute "meow"
```

### Reproducing the issue 

In the`src/cat.py` file:

```python
from Flask import current_app

meow = current_app.meow
```

The Flask subclass:

```python
from typing import Any

from flask import Flask
from flask_inflate import Inflate

class Cat(Flask):
    """
    Cat service implementation.
    """

    def __init__(self, import_name: str, meow: str,  *args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        """
        Construct the object.
        """
        super().__init__(import_name, *args, **kwargs)

        self.meow = meow

        Inflate().init_app(self)
```

Run mypy in the console:

```bash
$ mypy src
```

### Expected behaviour

```bash
$ mypy src
Success: no issues found in 1 source file
```

### Environment:

- Python version: 3.8.0
- Flask version: 2.0.0
- mypy version: 0.812

issues.title: before_request function for parent does not trigger for child route & child route returns 404
issues.body:
In this example, there are two routes: `/sample_parent` and `/sample_child`. The parent route is part of a parent blueprint; the child route is part of a child blueprint. The child blueprint is nested under the parent blueprint.

The expected behaviour is that both routes return a 403, because the parent blueprint has a before_request action that raises this.

The actual behaviour is that the parent route returns a 403, but the child route returns a 404.

The docs specifically state: `Blueprint-specific before request functions, etc. registered with the parent will trigger for the child.` [here](https://flask.palletsprojects.com/en/2.0.x/blueprints/#registering-blueprints)

It also confuses me that the route returns a 404 (not found) instead of a 200. I'd expect the route still to be found, but the before_request action not firing. This, however, could be related to [this issue](https://github.com/pallets/flask/issues/4037) which is already fixed in 2.0.1.


```python
from flask import Flask, Blueprint
from werkzeug.exceptions import Unauthorized

parent_bp = Blueprint("parent", __name__, url_prefix="/api")
child_bp = Blueprint("child", __name__)
parent_bp.register_blueprint(child_bp)


@parent_bp.before_request
def raise_error():
    raise Unauthorized


@parent_bp.route('/sample_parent', methods=['GET'])
def sample_parent():
    return 'ok', 200


@child_bp.route('/sample_child', methods=['GET'])
def sample_child():
    return 'ok', 200


def create_app(env=None):
    app = Flask(__name__)
    app.register_blueprint(parent_bp)
    return app


app = create_app()
app.run(port=5000, host="0.0.0.0")

```

When running `flask routes` I get:

```
Endpoint              Methods  Rule
--------------------  -------  -----------------------
parent.sample_parent  GET      /sample_parent
static                GET      /static/<path:filename>
```

Environment:

- Python version: 3.9
- Flask version: 2.0.0

issues.title: Url prefix duplicating when instanticiating multiple apps with nested blueprints
issues.body:
When using an app factory approach to create an app that has a blueprint with a url prefix, and a nested blueprint, the more times the app factory is called, the more times the parent url_prefix gets appended.

```
from flask import Flask, jsonify, Blueprint
from flask.views import MethodView


# Create a child blueprint with a simple view
class UsersView(MethodView):
    def get(self):
        return jsonify([]), 200

child_blueprint = Blueprint("child", __name__)
child_blueprint.add_url_rule("/user", view_func=UsersView.as_view("accounts"))

# Create a parent blueprint that registers the child blueprint
parent_blueprint = Blueprint("parent", __name__)
parent_blueprint.register_blueprint(child_blueprint)

# App factory
def create_app():
    app = Flask(__name__)
    app.register_blueprint(parent_blueprint, url_prefix="/api")
    return app

print("First app")
app = create_app()
print(app.url_map)

print("Second app")
app = create_app()
print(app.url_map)

print("Third app")
app = create_app()
print(app.url_map)
```
Output:
```
First app
Map([<Rule '/api/user' (HEAD, GET, OPTIONS) -> parent.child.accounts>,
 <Rule '/static/<filename>' (HEAD, GET, OPTIONS) -> static>])
Second app
Map([<Rule '/api/api/user' (HEAD, GET, OPTIONS) -> parent.child.accounts>,
 <Rule '/static/<filename>' (HEAD, GET, OPTIONS) -> static>])
Third app
Map([<Rule '/api/api/api/user' (HEAD, GET, OPTIONS) -> parent.child.accounts>,
 <Rule '/static/<filename>' (HEAD, GET, OPTIONS) -> static>])
```
In the above output you can see that the url_prefix gets appended an additional time each time the app factory is called

I would expect that the app factory could be called as many times as wanted, with the resulting url_map being the same each time

Environment:

- Python version: 3.8.1
- Flask version: 2.0.0

issues.title: Untyped decorator makes function untyped
issues.body:
When I run `mypy --strict` on the following file (named `flask_types.py`),

```python
from typing import Tuple

from flask import Flask

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.errorhandler(404)
def page_not_found(error: Exception) -> Tuple[str, int]:
    return str(error), 404
```

I get the following error:

```console
flask_types.py:7: error: Untyped decorator makes function "page_not_found" untyped
```

Instead, mypy should return no errors.

Using `--strict` (or the equivalent option in `setup.cfg`) in your tests might have caught an error like this, but given how new your type annotations are, I understand why you aren't using the setting yet.

The root cause appears to be that the implemented decorators often use `typing.Callable` in type annotations without any type parameters, which causes them to lose type information.

The fix for this specific issue is only a couple of lines (I have a prototype implemented locally), but I will try to add appropriate type parameters for `Callable` in as many places as possible. I expect to have a PR out for this in a couple of days.
Once I got a fix working for `errorhandler()`, mypy was able to find an error in my type annotations of `page_not_found()` as well as some internal issues in Flask itself, which I feel demonstrates how better typing would be useful here.

Environment:

- Python version: 3.7.9
- Flask version: 2.0.0
- mypy version: 0.812

---

PS: I really appreciate the new typing annotations in Flask! They seem like they took a lot of effort, and I have already found them useful. Thank you very much!

issues.title: Flask 2.0.0 Error Handler not called when Blueprint Name Contains a Period
issues.body:
When you have a blueprint, and it's name contains a `.` and it has error handlers registered, they are never called.

We have been using blueprints to help organize our application, and we have used `.` to help namespace the blueprint names. And we have registered error handlers on the blueprints. However, when an error occurs, they are never called.

Below is a simple example where you might have an app that has a UI and an API, and for UI errors you may have a custom error view, and for API errors you may want to return JSON.

```
from flask import Blueprint, Flask, jsonify

app = Flask(__name__)
ui = Blueprint("app.ui", __name__, url_prefix="/ui")
api = Blueprint("app.api", __name__, url_prefix="/api")


@ui.errorhandler(Exception)
def ui_error_handler(error):
    print("ui error handler called")
    return str(error)


@ui.get("/")
def ui_index():
    print("ui index called")
    raise Exception("this is an unhandled exception from the ui")


@api.errorhandler(Exception)
def api_error_handler(error):
    print("api error handler called")
    return jsonify(error=str(error))


@api.get("/")
def api_index():
    print("api index called")
    raise Exception("this is an unhandled exception from the api")


app.register_blueprint(ui)
app.register_blueprint(api)
```

Then when you run and do a get on one of the index endpoints you get:

```
 * Environment: production
   WARNING: This is a development server. Do not use it in a production deployment.
   Use a production WSGI server instead.
 * Debug mode: off
 * Running on http://127.0.0.1:5000/ (Press CTRL+C to quit)
api index called
[2021-05-13 13:14:48,849] ERROR in app: Exception on /api/ [GET]
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/lib/python3.9/site-packages/flask/app.py", line 2051, in wsgi_app
    response = self.full_dispatch_request()
  File "/lib/python3.9/site-packages/flask/app.py", line 1501, in full_dispatch_request
    rv = self.handle_user_exception(e)
  File "/lib/python3.9/site-packages/flask/app.py", line 1499, in full_dispatch_request
    rv = self.dispatch_request()
  File "/lib/python3.9/site-packages/flask/app.py", line 1485, in dispatch_request
    return self.ensure_sync(self.view_functions[rule.endpoint])(**req.view_args)
  File "app.py", line 29, in api_index
    raise Exception("this is an unhandled exception from the api")
Exception: this is an unhandled exception from the api
127.0.0.1 - - [13/May/2021 13:14:48] "GET /api/ HTTP/1.1" 500 -
```

You can see the `api index called` printed, but not the `api error handler called` printed which shows the error handler is never called.

```

The URL rule should be `/parent/child/` instead of `/`.

P.S. The URL prefix works fine if set the prefix by using `register_blueprint(url_prefix)`.

Environment:

- Flask version: 2.0
